results.message: What did your church do for its dead?

voice_event.speaker: lpc
voice_event.text:
We offered the sacrifice of the Mediator and gave alms in the church on their behalf. Augustine taught that these gifts help only those who earned that help while they lived. For the baptized dead who were very good, the offerings are thanksgiving. For those not very bad, they are propitiatory. For the very bad they do not help the dead at all, only console the living. Augustine wrote: “Nor can it be denied that the souls of the dead are helped by the devotion of their living friends. Those friends offer the sacrifice of the Mediator, or give alms in the church on their behalf. But these services help only those who earned, during their lives, the kind of merit that lets such services help them. For there is a way of life that is not so good that it needs no such help after death. Nor is it so bad that such help is of no use after death. There is also a kind of life so good that it does not need them. And there is one so bad that, when life is over, they give no help. So all merit or blame is gained in this life. It can either ease or worsen a person’s sufferings after this life. No one, then, should hope to gain after death the merit with God that he neglected to secure here.”

His own mother, Monica, asked one thing as she lay dying.

We can tell you what was decided and what was taught. We cannot tell you what an ordinary believer felt standing at a funeral, or what a family said to one another when someone died. That comes down to us almost nowhere.

names.name: Augustinius of Hippo Regius, presbyter 391, bishop 395/396-430

figures_used.bridge_line: Our bishop at Hippo. The people seized him and brought him to be made a presbyter while he wept. Later they pressed him into the bishop's office over his own refusal. He spent his last days weeping over psalms of penitence, while an army lay outside the walls.

dates.display: converted 386, baptised 387; seized by the congregation at Hippo and ordained presbyter against his own wishes in 391, weeping through it (Possidius, Vita IV); designated coadjutor and consecrated bishop of Hippo by Megalius, primate of Numidia, in 395/396, again amid popular acclamation (Possidius, Vita VIII); died 430, during the Vandal siege of Hippo
